Preliminaries We consider an episodic two-player Markov game (MG) with finite state and action spaces.1 Let ∆(X) denote the set of probability distributions over a finite set X. Such an MG is specified by a tuple (S, A, B, P, r, H), where • H is the number of steps in an episode; • S = ∪h∈[H+1] Sh is the state space, where there is a single terminal state in SH+1 ; • A = ∪h∈[H] Ah and B = ∪h∈[H] Bh are the action space for the max-player (learner) and the min-player (opponent) respectively; • P is a collection of unknown transition functions {Ph : Sh × Ah × Bh → ∆(Sh+1 )}h∈[H] . • r is the collection of reward functions {rh : Sh × Ah × Bh → [0, 1]}h∈[H] . In each episode k ∈ [K], the Markov game starts from an adversarially chosen initial state sk1 ∈ S1 . At the beginning of this episode, each player commits to a policy that may depend on the entire history of the previous k − 1 episodes. We denote our policy by µk = {µkh }h∈[H] and the opponent’s policy by ν k = {νhk }h∈[H] , where µkh : Sh → ∆(Ah ) and νhk : Sh → ∆(Bh ) are policies for step h. Neither player is allowed to modify its policy within an episode. At each step h ∈ [H], both players observe the current state skh and simultaneously select actions akh ∈ Ah drawn from µkh (skh ) and bkh ∈ Bh drawn from νhk (skh ), respectively. They then observe reward rhk := rh (skh , akh , bkh ), after which the environment transitions to the next state according to skh+1 ∼ Ph (·|skh , akh , bkh ). Importantly, at each step h ∈ [H], the opponent’s action bkh and policy νhk are unobservable to the learner. On the other hand, the opponent can observe the learner’s actions and is allowed to choose policies arbitrarily and adaptively as a function of the interaction history, knowing the MG and learner’s algorithm (but not their randomness) ahead of time. However, for ease of exposition, we sometimes restrict our attention to an oblivious opponent whose policies cannot depend on the learner’s past actions, and defer the details for a fully adaptive opponent to the appendix.
